Cotswold's population increased by around 8,000 between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021). This semi-automated article highlights some of the most notable changes among the local population.

The population reached nearly 91,000

Between the last two censuses (held in 2011 and 2021), the population of Cotswold increased by 9.6%, from just under 82,900 in 2011 to around 90,800 in 2021.

The population here increased by a greater percentage than the overall population of the South West (7.8%), and by a greater percentage than the overall population of England (up 6.6% since the 2011 Census).

In 2021, Cotswold was home to around 0.6 people per football pitch-sized piece of land, compared with 0.5 in 2011. This area was the joint third-least densely populated local authority area across the South West (after West Devon and Torridge).

This article generally uses percentages to enable comparisons over time and between areas. The percentage point change is also used to show the difference between the 2011 and 2021 percentages.

Population growth was higher in Cotswold than across the South West

An older Cotswold

Between the last two censuses, the average (median) age of Cotswold increased by three years, from 46 to 49 years of age.

This area had a higher average (median) age than the South West as a whole in 2021 (44 years) and a higher average (median) age than England (40 years).

The median age is the age of the person in the middle of the group, meaning that one half of the group is younger than that person and the other half is older.

The number of people aged 65 to 74 years rose by around 2,900 (an increase of 30.7%), while the number of residents between 35 and 49 years fell by around 1,800 (10.3% decrease).

The share of residents aged between 65 and 74 years increased by 2.2 percentage points between 2011 and 2021

Cotswold stood out from other areas for housing

The percentage of households in the social rented sector increased in Cotswold, but fell across England.

In Cotswold, the percentage of households in the social rented sector rose from 14.9% in 2011 to 15.4% in 2021, while across England it fell from 17.7% to 17.1%. During the same period, the regional percentage remained at 13.3%.

Private renting in Cotswold increased from 15.2% to 17.4%, while the rate of home ownership decreased from 65.7% to 65.1%.

The rate of social renting in Cotswold increased by 0.5 percentage points

Unpaid care in Cotswold

Cotswold saw the South West's second-largest percentage-point fall in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care (from 7.6% in 2011 to 4.3% in 2021). These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

Across the region, only Stroud saw a greater fall in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care (from 8.4% to 5.0%).

Every local authority area across the South West saw a fall in the proportion of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care, as the regional proportion fell from 7.5% to 4.7%.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and managed their provision of unpaid care, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people (aged five years and over) providing up to 19 hours of weekly unpaid care in Cotswold decreased by 3.3 percentage points

Health in Cotswold

In 2021, 53.6% of Cotswold residents described their health as "very good", increasing from 50.9% in 2011. Those describing their health as "good" fell from 34.5% to 33.0%. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

The proportion of Cotswold residents describing their health as "very bad" remained 0.7%, while those describing their health as "bad" was 2.6% (similar to 2011).

These data reflect people’s own opinions in describing their overall health on a five point scale, from very good to very bad.

Census 2021 was conducted during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived and rated their health, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

The percentage of people in very good health in Cotswold increased by 2.7 percentage points

Changing relationships in Cotswold

Cotswold saw the South West's joint third-largest percentage-point rise (alongside Torridge and South Somerset) in the proportion of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership (from 9.0% in 2011 to 9.8% in 2021).

Across the region, only Dorset (from 9.8% to 10.8%) and West Devon (from 9.6% to 10.5%) saw a greater increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership.

Across the South West, the percentage of people aged 16 years and over who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership increased from 9.8% to 10.1%, while the percentage in nearby Wiltshire increased from 9.5% to 10.0%.

These figures include same-sex marriages and opposite-sex civil partnerships in 2021, neither of which were legally recognised in England and Wales in 2011. Same-sex marriages have been legally recognised in England and Wales since 2014 and opposite-sex civil partnerships have been recognised since 2019.

The percentage of adults who had divorced or dissolved a civil partnership in Cotswold increased by 0.8 percentage points

Religion in Cotswold

In 2021, 36.7% of Cotswold residents reported having "No religion", up from 22.9% in 2011. The rise of 13.8 percentage points was the largest increase of all broad religious groups in Cotswold. Because the census question about religious affiliation is voluntary and has varying response rates, caution is needed when comparing figures between different areas or between censuses.

Across the South West, the percentage of residents who described themselves as having "No religion" increased from 29.3% to 44.1%, while across England the percentage increased from 24.8% to 36.7%.

In 2021, 55.7% of people in Cotswold described themselves as Christian (down from 68.7%), while 6.0% did not state their religion (down from 7.3% the decade before).

There are many factors that can cause changes to the religious profile of an area, such as a changing age structure or residents relocating for work or education. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses. Religious affiliation is the religion with which someone connects or identifies, rather than their beliefs or religious practice.

In 2021, 36.7% of usual residents in Cotswold reported having "No religion"

Cotswold residents' country of birth

In the latest census, around 79,100 Cotswold residents said they were born in England. This represented 87.1% of the local population. The figure has risen from just over 73,400 in 2011, which at the time represented 88.6% of Cotswold's population.

Wales was the next most represented, with just under 1,900 Cotswold residents reporting this country of birth (2.1%). This figure was up from just under 1,800 in 2011, which at the time also represented 2.1% of the population of Cotswold.

The number of Cotswold residents born in Scotland remained close to 1,500 between the last two census (from 1.8% of the local population in 2011 to 1.6% in 2021)

In 2021, 87.1% of Cotswold residents reported their country of birth as England

Unemployment in Cotswold

In 2021, 1.8% of Cotswold residents (aged 16 years and over) said they were unemployed. This figure decreased from 2.2% in 2011.

In 2021, just under 6 in 10 people (56.6%) said they were employed (excluding full-time students), compared with 59.0% in 2011. The percentage of retired Cotswold residents increased from 26.0% to 28.3%.

The decrease in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over (excluding full-time students) who were unemployed was greater across the South West (0.8 percentage points, from 2.9% to 2.1%) than in Cotswold (0.4 percentage points). Across England, the percentage fell by 1.1 percentage points, from 4.0% to 2.9%.

Census 2021 took place during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic, a period of rapid and unparalleled change; the national lockdown, associated guidance and furlough measures will have affected the labour market and our ability to measure it.

The percentage of people aged 16 years and over who were unemployed (excluding full-time students) in Cotswold decreased by 0.4 percentage points

Change in work hours

In 2021, 13.2% of Cotswold residents aged 16 years and over and in employment said they worked 15 hours or less per week. This figure increased from 12.3% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in seven people (14.3%) said they worked over 49 hours per week, compared with 17.5% in 2011. The percentage of adults in employment working 31 to 48 hours per week increased from 51.1% to 53.5%.

The increase in the percentage of people aged 16 years and over and in employment who said they usually worked 15 hours or less per week was greater in Cotswold (0.9 percentage points) than across the South West (0.5 percentage points, from 10.8% to 11.3%). Across England, the percentage increased by 0.6 percentage points, from 9.7% to 10.3%.

Working hours may have been affected by the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic.

The percentage of adults who worked 15 hours or less in Cotswold increased by 0.9 percentage points

National identity in Cotswold

In 2021, 4.2% of Cotswold residents did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK. This figure increased from 3.4% in 2011.

In 2021, 1.5% of residents identified with a UK and non-UK national identity, compared with 0.7% in 2011. The percentage of residents in Cotswold that identified as "British only" increased from 17.0% to 58.0%.

The increase in the percentage of people who did not identify with any national identity associated with the UK was greater across the South West (1.7 percentage points, from 4.4% to 6.1%) than in Cotswold (0.8 percentage points). Across England, the percentage increased by 1.7 percentage points, from 8.2% to 10.0%.

In Census 2021, “British” was moved to the top response option and this may have influenced how people described their national identity. For further information, please see our quality report.

The percentage of people who did not identify with at least one UK national identity in Cotswold increased by 0.8 percentage points

Family in Cotswold

Of Cotswold households, 20.3% included a couple but no children in 2021, down from 21.7% in 2011.

In 2021, just over one in six households (17.9%) included a couple with dependent children, compared with 19.3% in 2011. The percentage of single family households including a couple living with only non-dependent children increased from 5.6% to 5.9%.

This area had the region’s third highest percentage of households including a couple but no children. Across the region, only Isles of Scilly (23.8%) and West Devon (20.5%) had a higher percentage of households including a couple but no children.

Because of its small size, comparisons to Isles of Scilly should be made with caution.

The percentage of households including a couple without children in Cotswold decreased by 1.4 percentage points

Disability in Cotswold

In 2021, 4.9% of Cotswold residents were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. This figure decreased from 5.8% in 2011. These are age-standardised proportions.

Age-standardised proportions are used throughout this section. They enable comparisons between populations over time and across geographies, as they account for differences in the population size and age structure.

In 2021, just over 1 in 11 people (9.1%) were identified as being disabled and limited a little, compared with 8.7% in 2011. The proportion of Cotswold residents who were not disabled increased from 85.6% to 86.0%.

This area had the region’s second lowest proportion of residents who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot. Across the region, only Isles of Scilly, with 4.0%, had a lower proportion.

Census 2021 was undertaken during the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic. This may have influenced how people perceived their health status and activity limitations, and therefore may have affected how people chose to respond.

Caution should be taken when making comparisons between 2011 and 2021 because of changes in question wording and response options.

The percentage of people who were identified as being disabled and limited a lot in Cotswold decreased by 0.9 percentage points

Ethnic groups in Cotswold

In 2021, 1.5% of Cotswold residents identified their ethnic group within the "Mixed or Multiple" category, up from 0.8% in 2011. The 0.7 percentage-point change was the largest increase among high-level ethnic groups in this area.

Across the South West, the percentage of people from "Mixed or Multiple ethnic groups" increased from 1.4% to 2.0%, while across England the percentage increased from 2.3% to 3.0%.

In 2021, 96.3% of people in Cotswold identified their ethnic group within the "White" category (compared with 97.8% in 2011), while 1.3% identified their ethnic group within the "Asian, Asian British or Asian Welsh" category (compared with 1.0% the previous decade).

The percentage of people who identified their ethnic group within the "Other" category ("Arab" or "Any other ethnic group") increased from 0.1% in 2011 to 0.4% in 2021.

There are many factors that may be contributing to the changing ethnic composition of England and Wales, such as differing patterns of ageing, fertility, mortality, and migration. Changes may also be caused by differences in the way individuals chose to self-identify between censuses.
